| D34 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **Lance detached versions are the R7 mechanism**: a collection's Lance dataset has one mainline version (the empty version 1); every later Lance commit is detached (`_versions/d<id>.manifest`), built from exactly the parent collection manifest's `lance_version`, and the Loams manifest CAS is the only linearization point | Lance's mainline commit rebases onto newer versions even with no retries, and version paths are deterministic, so a zombie's or crashed writer's version would be absorbed or would block every later commit; detached versions have unique paths and never rebase | Approved (M1.1 plan, ruling 1) |
| D35 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **Loams GC owns Lance deletion; Lance cleanup is never run** (nor auto-cleanup). `CollectionGcRoots` computes Lance reachability from the Lance manifests of the retained chain and collects only Lance's known file classes | Lance cleanup lists only mainline manifests and would delete every file only detached versions reference once it is 7 days old | Approved (M1.1 plan, ruling 2; overview A15) |
| D36 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **Stable row ids join Lance and Tantivy**: splits store the Lance stable row id in a `_rowid` fast field, and typed fields exist only in Tantivy (Lance holds `_source`, system columns and vectors) | Row ids survive Lance compaction, so splits and the PK index never change when Lance compacts; Tantivy filters, sorts and aggregates, and ES fields may be single- or multi-valued, which has no natural Arrow type | Approved (M1.1 plan, rulings 4 and 8) |
| D37 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **The PK index is derived state** with a watermark (the manifest and `applied` offsets it reflects), written only after the manifest CAS and repaired from per-commit PK delta objects (or rebuilt from Lance) | The CAS is the commit point; the PK index may lag it by one commit, and the stream may be trimmed, so the deltas cannot be re-derived from it | Approved (M1.1 plan, ruling 7) |
| D38 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **Collection time travel**: every manifest is kept for `time_travel_retention` (24 h) after it is superseded, plus the last `keep_manifests`, with every object they reference; implicit streams are trimmed only below the oldest retained manifest | Pinned reads (ES PIT, Qdrant snapshots) need a manifest's objects and the stream tail after its offsets for as long as it is retained, with no metastore hold | Approved (M1.1 plan, ruling 12); amended by D90 (GC reachability counts every branch of a lineage, M2) |
| D39 (number assigned at merge) | 2026-09-24 | **Lucene-compatible analyzers** (`standard`, `english`, `simple`, `whitespace`, `keyword`), with the original Porter stemmer ported from Porter's C reference, not Porter2 | The BEIR gate (within 1 nDCG@10 of ES) depends on tokenization and stemming matching Lucene | Approved (M1.1 plan, ruling 25); amended by D93 (ES language analyzers, folding, pre-tokenized text and per-field k1 and b in M2) |

Postgres follows Lakekeeper's patterns (READ COMMITTED with explicit row locks in a fixed order, CAS as a conditional UPDATE with the row count checked, a commit-token row in the same transaction for unknown outcomes, separate read and write pools, sqlx with offline query checks). DynamoDB uses one table with the item layout and method mappings of §18 §2.3 (lazy partition heads, janitor-driven drops, `ClientRequestToken` on application retries). **`loams-meta-tidb`** (MySQL protocol through sqlx, not `tikv-client`) ships in **M6 and takes FoundationDB's M6 role**. Supersedes D47's FoundationDB clause | Most enterprises run Postgres, and Lakekeeper proves its patterns; DynamoDB is the AWS-native, serverless option and the store for the hosted control plane (M2.x); TiDB is scale-out, strongly consistent SQL with a managed offering | Approved (owner); FoundationDB dropped from the roadmap by D71; the `loams-meta-tidb` clause is superseded by D124 (`loams-meta-tikv` in R1); D260 confirms: no TiDB backend in any milestone |
| D59 | 2026-09-26 | **Relaxed `MetaStore` contract** (§18 §3): (a) `commit_wal` is atomic **per partition group** (a DynamoDB transaction group or a metastore shard, each committed idempotently through its own `(object, group)` record), not across all of a WAL object's partitions, and one stream's chunks of one object stay in one group while they fit; (b) the single monotonic metastore clock becomes **bounded-skew stamps** (the existing `ClockSkew` bound; WAL commit records pruned after `2·window + max_clock_skew`) plus **explicit GC-claim records**, checked by every command that makes an object reachable; (c) composite reads over DynamoDB follow **documented safe read orders**. Written into the trait docs and checked by the conformance suite and the linearizability checker in **M2's first task**, before any new backend. The openraft backend may keep its stronger behaviour; callers may rely only on the relaxed contract. Queries read one snapshot at the subscription manager's tick. Isolation is **snapshot isolation, with documents read by id promoted into the lock set** (`lock_keys`), so write skew is impossible on point reads and possible on index-range reads; serializable range reads are Q31. Commits default to async commit with 1PC, which cut commit p50 by roughly 30–50% against 2PC in the 2026-09-27 spike (indicative; loaded machine). A `commit_mode` switch falls back to 2PC for any component whose R1 gate fails with them, because `tikv-client` 0.4.0's async commit does not set `max_commit_ts`. Promotion closes the common read-modify-write case at the cost of one lock per read document; range serializability needs either guard keys (which serialize inserts into a bucket) or journal validation (which needs a proof), so it is decided with measurements in R2. A tailer per (node, app) reads the shard heads and new entries at each TSO tick and matches the written keys against the read-set index. A janitor deletes entries once every consumer has passed them and they are older than 10 min. TiKV CDC is a secondary path, not the invalidation source | The entries visible at tick `T` and not at `t` are exactly `head(t) < seq ≤ head(T)`, so no update is missed and no timing assumption is needed. But it needs copied private `tikv-client` stubs and a hand-written, region-by-region subscriber, and commit order waits on resolved ts, which advances about once a second. | D628 | 2026-10-04 | **Product-demo video recording is an external `ffmpeg` over an ffconcat list, not a streaming encoder and not a pure-Rust one.** `record::VideoRecorder` consumes the frames the docked panel already receives from `Page.startScreencast`; it starts no browser and opens no CDP connection of its own. Captured PNGs go to a scratch directory beside the output, one per frame, each with a `duration` directive taken from a **monotonic** (`std::time::Instant`) delta since the previous frame and clamped to `max_gap`; finalisation is a single `ffmpeg` run over that complete list, writing to `<output>.loams-partial.<ext>` which is fsynced and renamed into place. `.webm`/VP9 is the default container, `.mp4`/H.264 is also supported; the encoder is probed at `start` and never at finalisation. `LOAMS_FFMPEG_BIN` overrides the binary, mirroring the engine's own `LOAMS_OBSCURA_BIN`. **Out of scope by ruling: audio capture of any kind, editing, and post-processing.** | A streaming `ffmpeg -i pipe:0` was rejected on the correctness requirement, not on taste: a killed encoder leaves a container with no trailer and an incomplete index, which cannot be repaired. Here the frames survive the failure, so the same finalisation runs from `Drop` and produces the same playable file — one code path finalises, on the graceful path and on the panic path. A pure-Rust encoder was rejected because it needs **three** new dependencies (a PNG decoder, an encoder, a muxer), the only encoder-quality pure-Rust option being `rav1e`, which is heavyweight and slow on flat UI content. `ffmpeg` adds **zero** Rust dependencies, so `cargo deny` has nothing new to check and the `libvpx`/`libx264` licence questions attach to a distribution of ffmpeg rather than to Loams — a binary is invoked, exactly as the engine is. The costs are stated and accepted: `ffmpeg` is an optional runtime system dependency (the sidebar browser works without it; only recording is refused, with an error naming the variable), frames occupy disk for the recording's length, and encoding happens at stop. It is also the only option verifiable on a build machine, since `ffprobe` can open the result and `tests/recording.rs` asserts on the stream it reports | Proposed (owner, 2026-10-04); implementation `crates/loams-sidebar-browser/src/record.rs`, tests `crates/loams-sidebar-browser/tests/recording.rs` |
| D634 | 2026-10-04 | **Loams’ graph surface is GQL (ISO/IEC 39075), reached over Connect-RPC, and the reference engine is Grafeo embedded in the Fabric.** Six decisions, each for a stated reason. **(a) GQL, not Cypher.** GQL is the ISO standard and Cypher is Neo4j's dialect; a GQL connector is portable across Neo4j, Memgraph and anything GQL-conformant, which is what D354's "buy first" needs when the Rust ecosystem cannot supply it. Sink portability is the stronger half anyway, because writing nodes and edges varies far less between engines than traversals do. **(b) Grafeo is embedded, not a server.** It is written in Rust with no required C dependencies (`grafeo` 0.5.43 plus `grafeo-core`, `grafeo-engine`, `grafeo-adapters` and `grafeo-common`, all Apache-2.0, read on crates.io 2026-10-04), so Loams links it and calls it in process: no wire protocol, no Bolt, no second deployment unit, no auth to get wrong. The Fabric already runs one process with many sessions, and Grafeo has sessions with MVCC snapshot isolation, which is the same shape. **(c) No Bolt anywhere.** Bolt's Rust story is the strongest evidence here: `bolt-client` has had no release since December 2022 and its ecosystem is frozen with it, while the one maintained client, `neo4rs` 0.8.0, is Neo4j-specific rather than portable. Loams' internal connector-to-engine contract is **Connect-RPC**, already the engine's protocol, so reaching the engine over Bolt would add a second RPC stack to avoid one. *Correction (2026-10-16, owner-approved; the decision stands):* the premise that the Rust Bolt ecosystem is frozen is out of date: `boltr` 0.2.0 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, a pure-Rust Bolt 5.x library, crates.io 2026-04-11) is published by GrafeoDB, the organisation behind Grafeo. (c) stands on its other reason (Connect-RPC is the one contract) and on the owner's 2026-10-13 "do not add bolt"; Q926 asks when to revisit ([§48](48-loams-graph-production.md) §26.12). **(d) Neo4j is reached over its gRPC Query Service, not Bolt**, where that API covers what a connector needs; `neo4rs` is the fallback for what it does not, and its being Bolt-only is acceptable *for one vendor* precisely because Bolt is not the Loams-internal contract. **(e) Appendix A's Neo4j row was wrong and is corrected.** Both graph components Camel 4.22.1 ships, `camel-neo4j` and `camel-arangodb`, are `producerOnly: true`, so no route can read a graph through Camel, while A.3's row claimed `Source Y | Sink Y`. The row's source direction is now native, and Grafeo joins A.3 as its own row. **(f) Grafeo is a test target, not a foundation.** Its 23 701 crates.io downloads are two orders of magnitude below `neo4rs`, and its performance claims are self-reported; Loams depends on the *standard*, and Grafeo is the engine chosen because it can be embedded and tested, not because it is trusted as a foundation | §33 had one graph row whose source direction no runtime could serve. Measured: `camel-catalog` 4.22.1 marks both graph components `producerOnly`, and `apache/camel` at tag `camel-4.22.1` has no `components/camel-neo4j` at all despite the catalog advertising it as Stable. Research in [`graph-db-rust-spike.md`](../plans/graph-db-rust-spike.md) | High if wrong on Grafeo's maturity, which is why (f) separates the dependency from the standard: if Grafeo proves unmaintained the *standard* still stands and only the reference engine changes. `surrealdb` is excluded outright, because crates.io reports `license = "non-standard"`, which is not an SPDX id and so fails D359 |

| D636 | 2026-10-05 | **AP1d Task 2. The plugin action registry is the single description of each action, and the console enforces it with the primitives it already has.** `ActionRegistry` in `@loams/console-host` (`src/actions.ts`) holds a name, a description, an input schema, a risk and an execute closure; registration is non-transactional and returns a disposer, like `SlotRegistry.register` (`ctx.effect`), and a plugin may register only the names its manifest's new **`actions`** key lists (§37 §5.3's `slots` gate, applied to the callable surface). **(a) Enforcement is not re-implemented.** A method-backed action *derives* its permission from `METHOD_PERMISSIONS` through the existing `decideCall`, so a generated tool cannot be more permissive than the button behind it, and restating a different permission is refused at registration as drift; a local action names one of `PERMISSIONS`. At call time a method-backed action is decided by `decideCall` too, so **both** halves apply — the service must be in the plugin's `inject` list as well as the permission held — because checking only the permission would answer half of what the bridge answers. The registry can only ever **refuse**, which shortens the path to a refusal — OpenFGA and the credential broker (§39 §6) remain the boundary. **(b) A destructive action is never auto-approved, and a client-side approval gate may only refuse.** §39 §8 rule 1 makes `destructive` an `approve` and `write` in a *protected* environment an `approve`; rule 2 puts the gate in the credential broker and says the requester cannot approve their own request. So the gate is a **seam with no default**: with none wired, a destructive action resolves `approval_required` and `execute` never runs. The two checks a client can honestly make are that a decision came back and that its `decidedBy` is not the requester; everything else stays server-side. **(c) Every outcome is a resolved `{ok:true,value}` or `{ok:false,error:{code,message}}`, never a rejection**, because the draft reports a rejected `execute` as an opaque `UnknownError`, which would discard the code and message the caller needs. Codes are `unknown_action`, `permission_denied`, `approval_required`, `approval_denied`, `invalid_input`, `aborted`, `failed`. **(e) The two declarations the approval gate reads are required, not defaulted, and the approval proof is carried into `execute`.** A `write` whose environment was never resolved to be unprotected is **gated**, because §39 §8 rule 1's default is "allow *in non-protected environments*" — a claim about a *named* environment, which a call that named none has not made. An agent-driven surface must not read an absent environment as the permission it is asking for. And `risk` is **required** rather than defaulting to `read`, for the same reason: it is the one field that decides whether a person is asked, so an author who forgot it would otherwise get an un-gated action. §39 §8 rule 2 says a destructive call *carries* the approval id and the broker verifies it, so the id and its decider are passed to `execute` (`context.approval`) rather than checked and dropped — `execute` is the only thing that makes the call, and the broker has nothing to verify otherwise. | D639 | **The C++ SDK speaks Connect and gRPC-Web over HTTP, and does not depend on grpc++ or the `buf.build/grpc/cpp` plugin.** Design §44 §9 row 12 names `grpc++` as the library and issue #295 repeats it; the wire does not need it. One port serves the Connect protocol, gRPC and gRPC-Web (D600), and all four encodings the corpus records — `application/json`, `application/proto`, `application/grpc-web+proto`, `application/grpc-web+json` — are HTTP/1.1 `POST`s with a body. The generated surface is therefore **messages and service descriptors only**; the call path is hand-written over `loams::HttpTransport`, and `HttpTransport` is an interface so a caller who already links an HTTP/2 stack substitutes its own. **grpc++ is not installed on the machines or the CI runners that develop this repository**, and §9 row 12's own rule — gRPC "where no official Connect exists" (D612) — leaves a language with neither library speaking the HTTP transports rather than taking a dependency the build environment cannot satisfy | A C++ consumer who wants HTTP/2 multiplexing or the C++ server reflection APIs gets neither from this SDK. Both are reachable: the substitution seam is public, and `grpcurl` works against the server regardless of what the client is built from. The cost that is real is a second implementation if the owner later wants grpc++: `buf.gen.yaml` gains a plugin, `src/` gains a transport, and the conformance suite runs twice | Proposed (SDK2 Task 11); implementation `sdks/cpp/`, `DEPENDENCIES.md` |

Both are real regressions, and a committed file turns both into a green diff — the suite fails to run, or runs with a filter, and CI reads a report describing the last run that happened to write it. `check-languages.mjs` is only a gate if what it reads came out of the run in the same breath. | D651 | 2026-10-06 | **`run-test.sh` proves a test ran, rather than trusting the runner's exit status, and deletes the language's report before it starts.** Two independent ways a one-test run could be green without having run anything, both found by renaming `csharp_pagination_iterator` by one character and asking for the contract name. `dotnet test --filter` prints "No test matches the given testcase filter" and **exits 0**; and the check the script runs afterwards, `check-languages.mjs --check`, read the report an *earlier full run* had left on disk and found 28 of 28 in it — so a stale report vouched for a run that never happened. Two changes, and neither is specific to a language: the runner's output is captured and matched against the phrasings each runner uses for "no tests" (`dotnet test`, `ctest`, `pytest`, `go test`, `vitest`, gathered by running each against a name that does not exist), and the report is `rm`-ed first so only a write from *this* invocation can satisfy the check. A green run of zero tests is otherwise indistinguishable from a pass in every report that counts exits. Relatedly: `runOne` for C# now passes `-c Release`, because the default `Debug` is a second build and CI measures the other one. |

| D872 | 2026-10-13 | **Proposed** ([§52](52-loams-memory.md) §4; [MM1](../plans/2026-10-13-mm1-loams-memory.md)). **Stores and spaces.** A *memory store* is a resource in one namespace (one environment). A *space* is the unit of ownership, access and deletion inside a store, of one of five kinds: `user`, `project` (a repository is a project space bound to a repo), `org`, `agent`, `session`. **A read may compose up to 8 spaces; a write goes to exactly one.** Spaces never link to each other |
| D873 | 2026-10-13 | **Proposed** ([§52](52-loams-memory.md) §5; [MM1](../plans/2026-10-13-mm1-loams-memory.md)). **Physical layout: shared shards with a hard isolation invariant.** A store has shards; a shard is five managed collections and one linked graph. Each space is pinned to one shard at creation, or gets a **dedicated** shard. Every row and key carries the space id, every server-built query binds it, and no edge crosses spaces (**I-ISO**, §5.3) |
| D874 | 2026-10-13 | **Proposed** ([§52](52-loams-memory.md) §6.4; [MM1](../plans/2026-10-13-mm1-loams-memory.md)). **Facts are bi-temporal properties, invalidated and not deleted.** A fact has world time `[valid_at, invalid_at)` and system time `[recorded_at, expired_at)`. A contradiction closes the old fact's world interval; a correction closes its system interval; only *forget* deletes. Grafeo's `temporal` feature is **not** used (GR1 R9.6): time lives in properties, queried with `as_of` and `known_at` |
| D875 | 2026-10-13 | **Proposed** ([§52](52-loams-memory.md) §6.1; [MM1](../plans/2026-10-13-mm1-loams-memory.md)). **Episodes are the ground truth.** Every raw input is kept as an episode (non-lossy, Graphiti's model), and every fact names the episodes it came from. A fact with no remaining source episode is deleted (§7.4) |

| D1119 | 2026-10-19 | **Loams is fully open source; there is no open core.** The open-core boundary (D190, D220, D403, D440, D548, D550, D552, D557, D-SF-20, and in part the rows that apply it) is superseded. Everything, including billing-grade metering, billing, the hosted control plane and the commercial APIs, is Apache-2.0; nothing is withheld for a paid edition. Ostrium Labs' business is services: infrastructure efficiency and cost reviews, SLAs, support plans, migration help and help operating Loams (contact: support@ostriumlabs.org). The metering, billing and control-plane code of `loams-platform` is moving into the open repo now, under a separate design (§63, Loams Meter, being written); until each piece lands here, nothing in this repository depends on `loams-platform` (D551's one-way rule holds as a build rule, not a licensing one). Public docs may now name metering and billing; the no-metering CI guard (D552) is retired by that design. History is kept: superseded rows stay, marked | Owner: "Remove the open core. Everything is in OSS. We help companies with infra (make it efficient, SLAs, support) like a services company." One licence and one repository set are simpler to explain and to contribute to; services revenue does not depend on withholding code | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1120 | 2026-10-19 | **Loams Meter is the one metering and enforcement system, open, in Rust, in this repository** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §5): `loams-meter-core` (types, sans-I/O balance engine and lease allocator), `loams-meter-gate` (the in-process gate and emitter products link, with a `NoGate` default) and `loams-meter` (the `meter` role of `loams`, feature `meter`), exporters behind features. No runtime dependency on OpenMeter, Lago, Kafka or a ClickHouse server. The imported node agent becomes `loams-meter-agent`. Replaces `loams-platform`'s metering (D548's record) | The owner's draft of 2026-10-19 and D1119: metering and enforcement are different, enforcement is first-class; OpenMeter's Go, Kafka and ClickHouse stack is too heavy to self-host beside Loams, which already has a log, an analytical store and a metastore | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1121 | 2026-10-19 | **The usage event** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §6): a CloudEvent in the Loams profile that OpenMeter's ingest accepts unchanged: `subject` required (the billing subject, from the credential), JSON `data` (**amends D364's protobuf default** for `io.loams.dev.usage.*`), `type` `io.loams.dev.usage.<product>.<name>.v<major>`, `id` derived from the work, `tenantid` from the credential, and one new extension `loamslease` | OpenMeter compatibility makes exporting a pass-through; the House reads JSON with its own functions; deterministic ids make re-emission a duplicate | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1122 | 2026-10-19 | **Storage and dedupe** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §7): every event lands in the stream `_system/_meter` ( 32 partitions, keyed by `subject`); Loams' producers use D365's batched plain produce, external producers D270's ledger with a 24 h window. Duplicates are removed at the producer (stable ids), in the counter owner (a recent-keys set) and in the House (`ReplacingMergeTree` keyed `(subject, type, source, id)`, read with `FINAL`) | One stream, one order per subject; the ledger is too costly per event at usage rates (D365); `FINAL` on closed windows is exact and cheap | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1123 | 2026-10-19 | **Aggregation in the House** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §8): a close job writes minute, hour and day windows into `_meter.windows` (`ReplacingMergeTree(close_run)`) from `FINAL` reads; late events up to 24 h re-close windows; billing periods close 2 h after their end. **Only the House's windows are billed**; counters never are | The House is the source of truth and off the hot path; versioned window rows make a repeated or racing close job harmless | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1124 | 2026-10-19 | **The entitlement model is OpenMeter's** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §9): customers own subjects; meter → feature → entitlement (metered, boolean, static) → grant (amount, priority, effective time, expiry, rollover, recurrence); burn-down by priority, nearest expiry, then oldest, with promotional before included before prepaid; modes `hard_limit`, `soft_limit`, `overage_allowed`; plans as versioned entitlement templates; money as integer micros plus ISO 4217 (D374) | A model users and exporters already know; prepaid credit is spent last | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1125 | 2026-10-19 | **The enforcement path** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §10): products call `Gate::check` or `reserve`/`settle` at admission (House admission, the gateway's `pg`, `http`, `llm` and `mcp` modules, pg-control wake, jobs, functions, streams, Git, sandbox); a hit reads only local sharded counters (≤ 5 µs p99, target); a cold miss fetches a lease within a 50 ms deadline, then the policy decides | No network call per request; the cost of work known only afterwards is reserved and settled | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1126 | 2026-10-19 | **Multi-node leasing** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §11): the holder of a subject's `_system/_meter` partition lease is its counter owner (fenced epoch); it grants chunks of `clamp(1% of the allowance, min_chunk, remaining / (2 × holders))`, TTL 30 s, refresh 10 s, exact mode near the end; Doorman's learning mode for one TTL after a failover. Overshoot is accepted and bounded | Doorman's leases and Google Service Control's check-and-report, on the stream's existing partition leases | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1127 | 2026-10-19 | **Reconciliation** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §12): every 5 minutes and at period close, each owner rebases counters on House totals at the pipe's committed offsets (D769) and replays only the stream tail after them; drift above 1% of an allowance alerts | Splitting at the same offset counts every event exactly once | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1128 | 2026-10-19 | **Policy** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §13): no payment method → hard stop; overage only with a card, opt-in and under a mandatory spend cap; prepaid credits stop at zero; counters unavailable → free fails closed, paid fails open within its spend-cap headroom; thresholds at 80% and 100%; a hard stop refuses new work and lets running work finish | The owner's draft: enforcement is first-class, never invoice in arrears a tenant who has no card | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |
| D1129 | 2026-10-19 | **Threshold and lifecycle events go into `_system/_meter`** ([§63](63-loams-meter.md) §15): `io.loams.dev.meter.threshold.v1`, `…access.changed.v1`, `…entitlement.reset.v1`, `…grant.v1`, with ids that make re-emission a duplicate; a notifier delivers webhooks, email and console notices | One stream for usage and notifications, with history in the House | Approved (owner, 2026-10-19) |

The Rust engine reads every encoding the chDB House wrote: v2, `loams.ch.types`, nanosecond `long`s (D1572), JSON text, ClickHouse states, copy-on-write snapshots. A miss is a ruling that names the query and the HE3 work that closes it. Q1182's ClickBench bar (60–80 % of ClickHouse warm) stays HE3's | A budget per application query catches regressions that users would see; ClickBench stays internal (D414) | Proposed (HE1 lead, 2026-10-23; work proceeds on it until the owner rules) |
| D1804 | 2026-10-23 | **Proposed** ([§75](75-loams-house-engine.md) §15; plan [HE1](../plans/2026-10-21-he1-loams-house-engine.md) Task 23; extends D1564). **The oracle gates every engine task:** each HE1 and HE2 task adds cases under `conformance/clickhouse/oracle/corpus/he<N>/<task>/`, with expected answers taken at run time from `clickhouse-server` 26.9.2.8, never hand-written. The per-PR job `house-engine-oracle` runs them against the Rust engine's dev server over tables seeded from the oracle's own rows (no libchdb on the runner). A task merges with no `untriaged` entry and no `bug` entry that names it. Gaps owned by later tasks are `bug` entries with `task = "<N>"` | Semantic mismatches are the bulk of the work (§75 R4); catching them per task is cheaper than at the application gates | Proposed (HE1 lead, 2026-10-23; work proceeds on it until the owner rules) |
| D1805 | 2026-10-23 | **Proposed** ([§75](75-loams-house-engine.md) §7.6; plan [HE1](../plans/2026-10-21-he1-loams-house-engine.md) Task 37). **Settings on the Rust engine:** every setting the House front accepts is classed by the engine as *honoured* (it behaves as ClickHouse's does), *no-op* (performance or chDB internals only, with the reason recorded) or *refused* (`115`/`164`). A setting that changes results and is not honoured is refused at any value other than its default, never ignored. | Q32 | ~~MVCC GC for txn-API keyspaces: does TiKV honour keyspace-level safe points set through PD's GC-state RPCs, or must a `unified` GC TiDB run per cluster; will `tikv-client` accept a patch exposing keyspace GC (§20 §9.3, D122)~~ **Answered by R1 Task 0 (2026-09-27, `docs/plans/r1-dependency-spike.md`): no.** PD v8.5.8 has no GC-state RPCs (`AdvanceTxnSafePoint`/`GetGCState` answer `Unimplemented`), and TiKV v8.5.8 reads only the cluster safe point: a keyspace safe point set with `UpdateGCSafePointV2` was ignored for 90 s, while the cluster path (`UpdateServiceGCSafePoint` + `UpdateGCSafePoint`) dropped old versions within 10 s. TiKV serves reads below the safe point without an error. Loams’ GC loop therefore acts as the cluster's GC worker for every keyspace, with barriers as PD service safe points, and `loams-tikv` refuses reads older than the GC window (R1 plan rows R5–R7). Per-keyspace GC returns when a pinned PD release ships the GC-state API. Still open: whether `client-rust` accepts a patch exposing GC safe points (R1 exit report) | Eng | Answered (R1 Task 0); upstream patch: R1 exit report |
